cards.title: Jeff Shute
cards.sub: 22 May 2012 - SIGMOD, first author of the F1 talk deck
cards.prompt: Google's ad backend was sharded by customer. Who leads the author list on the SIGMOD 2012 talk deck cataloguing what that legacy system could not do, and what did the deck say the team therefore had to do about data growth?
cards.answer: Jeff Shute. The deck grouped the limitations as availability, scaling and functionality - no cross-shard transactions or joins, and rebalancing shards 'extremely difficult and risky' - and said the team therefore had to 'limit size and growth of data stored in database'.
cards.body: First author of both F1 papers and of the slide deck listing what AdWords was escaping. The Spanner paper's acknowledgements thank 'the F1 team, and Jeff Shute in particular' for work on the data model - the hierarchy that ended up making the advertiser a root row.

cards.title: The last resharding
cards.sub: concluded before 2011 - Google AdWords' sharded MySQL
cards.prompt: AdWords' MySQL was sharded by customer. Name the duration of the last resharding, how broadly it had to be coordinated, and the two things the team gave up rather than run it again.
cards.answer: Over two years of intense effort, with coordination and testing across dozens of teams to minimize risk. Rather than repeat it, they capped growth on the MySQL database and displaced data into external Bigtables - losing transactional behavior over that data and the ability to query across all of it.
cards.body: Tens of terabytes, small for its era, but cut by customer - so growth meant re-deciding which shard each customer lived on and moving them while the database billed advertisers. The Spanner paper calls resharding it 'extremely costly' and the operation 'too complex to do regularly'.

cards.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database, OSDI 2012
cards.sub: Corbett, Dean, Ghemawat, Hsieh et al. - section 5.4, 'F1'
cards.prompt: The Spanner OSDI paper is read for TrueTime, but one section prices the system F1 replaced. Which section is it, what sharding rule does it quote, and what is the first reason it gives for the F1 team adopting Spanner?
cards.answer: Section 5.4, titled 'F1'. The rule: the MySQL sharding scheme 'assigned each customer and all related data to a fixed shard'. The first reason listed: 'Spanner removes the need to manually reshard'.
cards.body: Twenty-six authors, OSDI 2012. Section 5.4 also reports F1's deployment - five replicas, two on the US west coast and three on the east - and a table of directory-fragment counts showing the vast majority of customers still land on a single server.

cards.title: The advertiser became the root row
cards.prompt: AdWords spent over two years unable to re-cut by customer, then moved to a different database entirely. What happened to the customer key in the new schema, and what does a single Spanner directory typically hold?
cards.answer: It was promoted, not dropped. F1 made the advertiser a root table, Customer, with Campaign and AdGroup clustered beneath it; a root row and all its descendant rows live in one Spanner directory, and each directory typically corresponds to one customer.
cards.body: The F1 paper states the shard-key rule plainly: 'most transactions are typically updating data for a single advertiser at a time, so we made the advertiser a root table (Customer) and clustered related tables under it.' The migration did not escape the key. It wrote the key into the schema.
